title: Arithmetic sequences and fixed increments
transcript: In an arithmetic sequence each new term adds the same difference. The term number counts entries, but the changes happen in the gaps between entries. For a total of several terms, pair values from the two ends. Their sums are equal.

AMC practice can hide a fixed increment in a seating plan, a stack or a pattern of growing figures. Check whether the differences are constant. A Rossmoyne style question may need a total without listing every term. Pairing gives a short calculation and a reason.
A list starts at five and increases by four each time. What are the first four terms? Count the starting number as the first term.
Add four three times after the starting value. That produces five, nine, thirteen and seventeen. There are four terms but only three gaps. The fixed step is the size of each gap.
A sequence has first term five and common difference four. What is term seventeen? Work out how many gaps separate that term from the first.

Term seventeen is sixteen steps beyond term one. The total increase is that number of steps times four. Add the first term. The requested term is sixty-nine. Check the rule would give five at term one.
A theatre section starts with five seats in its first row. Each new row contains four more than the row before it. There are fourteen rows. Find the total number of seats.

The last row contains fifty-seven, after thirteen increases. Pair the first row with the last. Every pair totals sixty-two. Moving inward adds four to one end and removes four from the other. There are seven pairs. Multiply by the common pair total to get four hundred and thirty-four seats.

A check is to imagine the rows redistributed evenly. The mean of the first and last values is the mean row length. Multiplying that mean by all fourteen rows gives the same total, four hundred and thirty-four seats.

The starting value occupies term one. A later position needs one fewer step than its term number. If the step changes, arithmetic-sequence formulas no longer apply. Check the first few differences before summing.

Write the first term and common difference. For a particular term, count the gaps before multiplying. For a sum, check the last term and whether there is an unpaired centre. Pair opposite ends to verify the total.
